sections.heading: The AT Protocol
sections.text: The AT Protocol (ATProto) is a decentralized networking protocol for social applications. It provides portable identity, interoperation between services, and a shared data model so that content and relationships are not siloed per app. This page is the technical overview in the shape that Boris cares about: the pieces that let a Boris-built static site become an on-network publication. For the Boris side, see Boris; for the loop that ties them together, see Standard.site — the Boris/ATProto loop.

sections.heading: The pieces Boris touches
sections.text: ATProto has several layers; the ones that matter for a published site are: DIDs — the portable, verifiable identifier that owns records. PDS — the Personal Data Server that hosts the account's repository of records and speaks the HTTP API. Records — typed JSON blobs stored in the repository under a + . Lexicons — the schemas that define record shapes (the family is what Boris publishes). Auth — two write paths: OAuth + DPoP (granular scopes) and the app-password (broad account write, Bearer). AppView / indexer — read-side services that aggregate records for discovery (non-normative for publication).

sections.heading: DIDs
sections.text: A DID is a self-certifying, portable identifier. ATProto uses (the PLC method, the dominant production method) and (DNS-anchored). A DID resolves to a DID document that points at the account's PDS and authorization server. Portability means the owner can move the account to a different PDS while keeping the same identifier and records. This site's profile ( ) is wired to the real identity (handle ), which resolves to the PDS at and the authorization server .

sections.heading: PDS and the HTTP API
sections.text: The Personal Data Server hosts the account's repository. It speaks an HTTP API (XRPC) for reading and writing records. A write to a PDS goes through: Discovery — resolve the DID to a PDS origin and authorization server metadata (RFC 9728). Authorization — obtain a credential that authorizes the write. The write — / / against the PDS. Readback — fetch the record by its AT-URI to confirm it landed. An AT-URI ( ) is the canonical address of a record. It is stable across moves because it is keyed by the DID, not the PDS host.

sections.heading: Records and lexicons
sections.text: A record is a typed JSON value stored at + under the owner's DID. The collection name namespaces the record's lexicon (e.g. , ). A lexicon defines the record's fields and validation rules. The family is small and deliberate: (rkey ) — the root pointer. It carries the site's production and , and ties the DID to a deployed origin. (one rkey per page) — a per-page record that points into the published tree. This is the shape Boris projects and publishes. dumps the canonical payloads offline (see the Standard.site — the Boris/ATProto loop guide).

sections.heading: Verification surface
sections.text: Because a record points a DID at a URL, publication is verifiable: a reader fetches the DID's record, learns the URL, and checks that the URL serves what the record claims. Boris's cross-checks the built tree against this projection offline — it confirms the head links and the file are consistent before any network write.

sections.heading: The two write paths
sections.text: ATProto offers two ways to authorize a write, and Boris supports both. They are not interchangeable, and the choice matters operationally.

sections.heading: OAuth + DPoP (granular scopes)
sections.text: The primary, scoped path. A client requests granular repository scopes (e.g. , ) via OAuth, and proves possession of the token with DPoP (RFC 9449, Demonstrating Proof of Possession). Each write is signed with a DPoP proof and a server-issued nonce. Pros: least privilege — the grant is scoped to specific collections, and the token binds to a key the client holds. Cons: requires a PDS and authorization server that implement the granular scopes and the DPoP nonce flow correctly. Operational note (recorded 2026-08-27): against / PDS instances, the OAuth + DPoP write path fails at the DPoP nonce layer with , reproducibly, on a freshly signed-in session. Read-side discovery and token exchange succeed; the record writes are rejected. See Test Runs for the full finding. This means OAuth writes currently need a self-hosted PDS that grants the granular collection scopes.
sections.code: repo:site.standard.document repo:site.standard.publication bsky.social bsky.network InvalidNonce

sections.heading: App-password (broad write, Bearer)
sections.text: The opt-in fallback. An app-password is a long-lived, broad-write credential (a Bearer token) that works on . Boris reads it once from stdin only — never from argv, profile, or environment. Pros: works against the dominant production PDS today; completes the full create/readback/delete round-trip. Cons: broad account write within its scope — the grant is not collection-scoped, so it must be used with a dedicated, disposable test identity and revoked after use. Operational note (recorded 2026-08-27): the app-password path fully passed a live smoke against a throwaway test identity ( / ): discovery, authorization, write (publication + document, unique rkeys), readback (AT-URI + value + CID verified for both records), and cleanup (both deleted, zero residue). See and Test Runs. The production identity for this site is now ( , PDS ).

sections.heading: Boris
sections.text: Boris is a single native binary — a content compiler written in Zig (currently , built with Zig 0.16.0 for Darwin-arm64). It takes a directory of Markdown (or Textile/Cooklang) and produces, in one pass, a verified static HTML site, a frozen content graph, a search index, and a publication proof pack. It is not a framework, has no runtime, and runs no JavaScript on the output. Everything is frozen at build time. This page is the technical overview. The operator's manual for the ATProto side is Standard.site — the Boris/ATProto loop; the AT Protocol background is The AT Protocol.

sections.heading: Build pipeline
sections.text: A build pass produces, for one HTML target: — the rendered pages, each wrapped in the layout. — copied theme assets (CSS, images, etc.). — a frozen search index derived from the committed HTML page set. — the publication proof pack (see below). The build is deterministic: the same input + profile + environment produces byte-identical output, which is what makes the proof pack's SHA-256 digests meaningful.

sections.heading: The proof pack
sections.text: Every HTML build writes . This is the heart of Boris's integrity model — it pins what was built, what was checked, and what can be claimed as a result. The pack has four artifacts plus an presentation: — the inventory. Every committed file in the target gets a , ( , , , , , ), , and . — the checks that ran, their status, coverage, and findings. The three core checks are (every artifact's bytes+sha256 match), (structural/route/ fragment/duplicate-ID audit of HTML pages), and (the search index matches the committed HTML page set). — the verifiable claims, each grounded in a check's evidence and explicitly limited by a set of limitations. A claim is only when its supporting check passed with complete coverage. — the full relationship graph (nodes + edges) that connects targets → artifacts → checks → claims → limitations. The presentation at renders the pack as a human-readable report with status banners and tables.
sections.code: dist/_boris/proof/ index.html artifacts.json path kind html-page theme-asset rendered-search sitemap rss llms bytes sha256 checks.json artifact-integrity rendered-html rendered-search claims.json verified touches.json _boris/proof/index.html

sections.heading: What the claims mean — and don't
sections.text: A verified claim is deliberately scoped. The limitations are part of the claim, not a footnote: — the claim describes one local target after commit; it says nothing about other targets or environments. — local generation cannot verify deployed behavior. — no a11y audit was performed. — no writing-quality judgment. — deterministic bytes on one recorded environment are not universal reproducibility. — an omitted projection is explicitly unverified, not certified. This is the "conductor rule": what was not inspected remains explicitly unverified. The proof pack never overclaims.

Context mode ( ) — a single bounded context bundle (byte-capped via ). — a deterministic export for LLM consumption. — a deterministic RSS 2.0 feed. — a deterministic in the HTML target. — restrict RAG/context to an entity id or collection prefix. sections.heading: Boris's design stance
sections.text: Three commitments shape the tool: Publication truth is the production URL. The deployment origin is not incidental — it is the anchor that ties identity to a built tree. records it; enforces it offline. Explicit, never implicit. Nothing is written to the network without an explicit command and a stored session. The build and proof pack are offline and deterministic; publication is a separate, gated, manual act. Fail closed on drift. A committed makes fail-closed against drift. A to a missing page fails the build. An omitted projection is explicitly unverified, not silently certified. These are why the proof pack's limitations read the way they do: Boris does not claim what it did not inspect. The next page, The AT Protocol, explains the network side that the standard-site family publishes to.

sections.heading: T-01 — Offline plan
sections.text: Produces a deterministic record projection: the record, the verification project path, and document exclusions. Documents are excluded until they have a date; exclusion reasons are recordable and part of the expected output. Pass when: output is stable across repeated runs with identical input/profile, all s and values match, and no network/credential is touched.

sections.heading: T-02 — Canonical records
sections.text: Dumps the full canonical record payloads (e.g. ). Pass when: the payload is byte-stable, / / are correct, and it runs fully offline.

sections.heading: T-03 — Verify built tree

sections.heading: T-07 — Publish
sections.text: One-shot publish from a stored session; reconcile + rotate-or-die on refresh. With a committed it is fail-closed on drift against that plan. Pass when: is emitted with the created , the record is readable back from the PDS, and pruning only occurs with explicit authority.

sections.text: Manual, opt-in, never in CI. Bounded, leaves no residue. Creates two records under unique rkeys, readback-verifies them against the PDS, deletes them, and emits a . Uses a clock-derived namespace by default; pass for a throwaway prefix. Optional: to verify the served origin, for a non-normative AppView observation. Pass when: both records are written and read back, both are deleted, and the result artifact records the whole lifecycle.

sections.heading: Acceptance criteria
sections.text: T-01/T-02 — Deterministic output: two runs with the same input and profile must produce byte-identical plans and canonical record payloads. All hashes and s are stable across runs. T-03 — cross-checks the built head links and the project file offline, and fails on drift. T-04/T-05 — A dedicated test identity authorizes without touching real account data. Credentials are accepted only via stdin, never argv/profile/env. T-06 — lists DID/flavor/PDS without secrets; securely erases the stored session. T-07 — One-shot publish from the stored session, reconcile + rotate-or-die on refresh, and a committed-plan fail-closed guard. T-08 — Smoke creates two records under unique rkeys, readback-verifies them, deletes them, and emits a artifact. Runs against a throwaway namespace and leaves no residue.

sections.heading: Boris on ATProto
sections.text: This site is a hands-on technical overview of Boris — the Zig content compiler — and the AT Protocol surface it publishes to. It is also a living demo: every page here is compiled by Boris itself, and the whole site can be projected onto the lexicon and published to an ATProto PDS. The docs are an artifact of the tool under description.
sections.code: standard.site

sections.heading: What you are looking at
sections.text: Boris is a single native binary that turns a directory of Markdown files into a verified static site. It is not a framework and it has no runtime: it produces frozen HTML, a frozen graph, a frozen search index, and a publication proof pack — a set of artifacts, checks, and claims whose hashes pin what was built. The AT Protocol gives that frozen site a place to live on the network: a record that points a DID at a production URL, and records that point at individual pages. The three ideas this site explores: Boris — what Boris is, how the build pipeline works, what the proof pack guarantees, and how IR/RAG/context exports turn the same content into machine-readable corpora. The AT Protocol — the AT Protocol in the shape Boris cares about: DIDs, PDSes, XRPC, records, lexicons, and the two auth paths (OAuth + DPoP vs app-password) that gate writes. Standard.site — the Boris/ATProto loop — the meta guide: how to take a Boris-built site and project, verify, authorize, and publish it to ATProto with the family. This page is the operator's manual, and it is exercised by the very site it documents.
sections.code: site.standard.publication site.standard.document boris standard-site

sections.heading: Why this is interesting
sections.text: A static site generator that emits a cryptographic proof pack, wired to a decentralized identity and record store, is a different shape from a typical "deploy to a CDN" pipeline. The production URL is not an incidental detail — it is the anchor that ties a DID to a built tree, and Boris treats it as publication truth. projects the records offline and deterministically; cross-checks the built output against that projection offline; only then does an explicit, session-gated write to the network. This site is built with two commands (the HTML build with profile + sitemap, then the standalone export): The build emits plus: — the publication proof pack (artifacts, checks, claims, touches). Inspect it at after a build — it renders the artifacts, checks, and claims as a report. — the frozen search index. — the verification surface (the publication record's AT-URI, for readers who fetch the well-known URL to confirm the DID points at this origin). — a deterministic sitemap of all 9 pages under . — a deterministic LLM-consumable index of every page with its title and summary.

sections.heading: The meta loop
sections.text: This site is recursively self-describing: The Markdown in is the source. compiles it to and writes the proof pack, the well-known file, and the sitemap. exports from the same content graph. projects the records offline using (the DID + URL that anchor publication). cross-checks the built tree offline. + writes to a real PDS, gated by a stored session and a committed-plan fail-closed guard. Steps 1–5 are offline, deterministic, and CI-safe. Step 6 is explicit, manual, and never implicit. The whole loop is documented in Standard.site — the Boris/ATProto loop and exercised by the test matrix in Testing Plan, whose results are logged in Test Runs.

sections.heading: Standard.site — the Boris/ATProto loop
sections.text: This is the meta guide. It documents how to take a Boris-built site and project, verify, authorize, and publish it to the AT Protocol via the family — and the site you are reading is itself produced by that loop. Every command below is run against this site. The two references this page ties together: Boris (the compiler and proof pack) and The AT Protocol (the network pieces). The procedures are in Standard.site Test Procedures; the run log in Test Runs.
sections.code: boris standard-site

sections.heading: The loop
sections.text: The first row (build, plan, verify, records) is offline, deterministic, and CI-safe — no network, no credentials. The second row (login, publish, smoke) is live, explicit, and session-gated — nothing is written to the network without an explicit command.
sections.code: ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ content/ ──boris build──▶ dist/ + _boris/proof │ │ (offline, deterministic) │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ ┌─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ standard-site plan standard-site verify standard-site records (offline project) (offline cross-check) (offline payloads) │ │ └──────────┬──────────┘ ▼ standard-site login (live, session stored 0600) │ ▼ standard-site publish (live, explicit, plan-guarded) │ ▼ standard-site smoke (live, manual, bounded, no residue)

sections.heading: Step 1 — build (offline)
sections.text: The build is two commands: the HTML build (with profile, sitemap) and the standalone export: The first command produces the HTML target, the proof pack under , the verification file, and . The file contains the publication record's AT-URI ( ) so a reader who fetches can confirm the DID points at this origin. The sitemap lists all 9 pages under . The second command exports , a deterministic LLM-consumable index of every page with its title and summary. See Boris for what the pack guarantees. This is the step you repeat on every content change.
sections.code: llms.txt boris build --input content --html-dir dist --theme themes/boris \ --profile standard-site.json --sitemap --site-url https://boris.filed.fyi/ boris --input content --llms --llms-path dist/llms.txt dist/_boris/proof/ .well-known/site.standard.publication dist/sitemap.xml .well-known at://did:plc:jiokpoojzqntdpyw5xvfr7rv/site.standard.publication/self https://boris.filed.fyi/.well-known/site.standard.publication https://boris.filed.fyi/ llms.txt

sections.heading: Dated documents project as records
sections.text: A page projects as a record only when its frontmatter carries a date (full UTC: ) and a non-empty . Without both, the page appears in the plan's with reason . Every page on this site now carries both, so all 9 project as document records — 10 records total (1 publication + 9 documents).
sections.code: site.standard.document published_at YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ summary exclusions missing-date

sections.heading: Step 2 — plan (offline)
sections.text: Emits a deterministic projection of the records that would be published: the record (rkey ), the 9 records (one per dated page), the verification file path, the document exclusions (now empty — every page is dated), and the verification surface projection. No network, no credentials. The output is byte-stable across runs with identical input + profile. This is what you commit and diff against.
sections.code: boris standard-site plan --profile standard-site.json --out evidence/plan.json site.standard.publication self site.standard.document .well-known/site.standard.publication

sections.heading: Step 3 — records (offline)
sections.text: Dumps the full canonical record payloads — the exact JSON that would be written to the PDS. For a fresh site this is just the publication record ( ); once pages carry dates, it includes the records too.
sections.code: boris standard-site records --profile standard-site.json --out evidence/records.json self {"url":..., "name":...} published_at site.standard.document

sections.heading: Step 4 — verify (offline)
sections.text: Cross-checks the built tree against the profile projection: the head links in the HTML and the project file. Fails on drift. Before a real origin and dated documents exist, correctly reports (well-known , empty). This is the fail-closed gate doing its job, not a tool failure — see the insight in Test Runs. T-04 passes once the production origin is configured and documents carry dates.
sections.code: boris standard-site verify --profile standard-site.json --dist dist --out evidence/verify.json .well-known/site.standard.publication verify overall_passed: false missing documents

sections.heading: Step 5 — login (live)
sections.text: Persists a session to a store. lists DID/flavor/PDS with no secrets. The app-password is read once from stdin only — never argv, profile, or environment. Finding: on , OAuth + DPoP writes fail with ; the app-password path is the supported live target. See The AT Protocol and Test Runs.
sections.code: # OAuth + DPoP path (granular scopes; needs a compliant PDS) boris standard-site login --did did:plc:jiokpoojzqntdpyw5xvfr7rv # app-password path (broad write; works on bsky.social; secret via stdin) boris standard-site login --app-password --handle boris.filed.fyi 0600 sessions bsky.social InvalidNonce boris standard-site sessions boris standard-site logout --handle <test-handle>

sections.heading: Step 6 — publish (live, explicit)
sections.text: One-shot publish from the stored session. Reconciles the live repository state, rotates tokens (rotate-or-die on refresh failure), and writes the projected records. With a committed , it is fail-closed on drift between the profile and the committed plan. Pruning only occurs with explicit authority (ANDs with the profile flag). Nothing is deleted implicitly.
sections.code: boris standard-site publish --profile standard-site.json --out evidence.json --plan PATH --prune prune

sections.heading: Step 7 — smoke (live, manual, never in CI)
sections.text: A bounded, manual interop check — never run in CI. It creates two records under unique rkeys, readback-verifies them against the PDS (AT-URI + value + CID), then deletes them, leaving no residue. Optional checks the served origin; observes a non-normative AppView. This site's last smoke (2026-08-27, app-password path, against the earlier throwaway identity) passed across discovery, authorization, write, readback, and cleanup. See and Test Runs. A fresh smoke against the live identity is the next planned run.

sections.heading: The meta point
sections.text: This page is part of the site it documents. The Markdown source lives at ; compiles it into the HTML you are reading and includes it in the proof pack's artifact inventory; would project it as a record (once it carries a date); would cross-check its head links offline; and would write it to the PDS, gated by the stored session and the committed-plan guard. Every command in this loop is reproducible from the kit. Start with Getting Started to add a page, Publishing for the profile details, and Standard.site Test Procedures for the per-surface procedures.
